paras.text: Alkanes are quite inert and unreactive towards most of the reagents under ordinary conditions. That is why they are also called paraffins. The word paraffin is derived from Latin words parum affinis (little affinity or little reactivity) and testifies to the low reactivity of alkanes. The little reactivity of alkanes is attributed to saturated nature and presence of non-polar C–C and C–H sigma bonds. Consequently polar reagents do not react with alkanes under normal conditions. Furthermore, the C–H and C–C bonds are strong bonds and hence alkanes are relatively stable to common reagents such as acids, alkalies, reducing and oxidizing agents etc. at ordinary conditions. However, they can react with several reagents, if the right conditions are used. The characteristic reactions of alkanes are free-radical substitution reactions.

paras.text: (b) Cycloalkanes
paras.urdu: (b) سائیکلوالکینز

paras.text: Cycloalkanes resemble alkanes in their chemical behaviour except for cyclopropane and cyclobutane. The strength of bond and hence the stability, depends on the extent of overlap of orbitals. In the case of cyclopropane and cyclobutane, the extent of overlap of orbitals is not maximum due to greater angle strains and are unstable (Section 16.2.3.2). Cyclopropane undergoes ring opening reactions with several reagents to give open chain addition product. Cyclobutane, having less angle strain than that of cyclopropane, is more stable and hence it undergoes ring opening reaction only under severe conditions. For example, hydrogenation of cyclopropane and cyclobutane to corresponding open chain alkanes in the presence of nickel catalyst, occurs at 80°C and 200°C respectively. Higher members are even more stable and do not undergo ring opening reactions. Instead, they resemble open chain alkanes in reactivity and undergo only radical substitution reactions.

16.2.4 Relative Stability and Reactivity

(a) Alkanes

Alkanes are quite inert and unreactive towards most of the reagents under ordinary conditions. That is why they are also called paraffins. The word paraffin is derived from Latin words parum affinis (little affinity or little reactivity) and testifies to the low reactivity of alkanes. The little reactivity of alkanes is attributed to saturated nature and presence of non-polar C–C and C–H sigma bonds. Consequently polar reagents do not react with alkanes under normal conditions. Furthermore, the C–H and C–C bonds are strong bonds and hence alkanes are relatively stable to common reagents such as acids, alkalies, reducing and oxidizing agents etc. at ordinary conditions. However, they can react with several reagents, if the right conditions are used. The characteristic reactions of alkanes are free-radical substitution reactions.

(b) Cycloalkanes

Cycloalkanes resemble alkanes in their chemical behaviour except for cyclopropane and cyclobutane. The strength of bond and hence the stability, depends on the extent of overlap of orbitals. In the case of cyclopropane and cyclobutane, the extent of overlap of orbitals is not maximum due to greater angle strains and are unstable (Section 16.2.3.2). Cyclopropane undergoes ring opening reactions with several reagents to give open chain addition product. Cyclobutane, having less angle strain than that of cyclopropane, is more stable and hence it undergoes ring opening reaction only under severe conditions. For example, hydrogenation of cyclopropane and cyclobutane to corresponding open chain alkanes in the presence of nickel catalyst, occurs at 80°C and 200°C respectively. Higher members are even more stable and do not undergo ring opening reactions. Instead, they resemble open chain alkanes in reactivity and undergo only radical substitution reactions.

16.3 Radical Substitution Reactions

16.3.1 Overview

Substitution reactions are those reactions in which an atom or group of atoms, attached to the carbon in a molecule is replaced by another atom or group of atoms. A substitution reaction may be initiated by free radical, nucleophile or electrophile. Substitution reactions which involve free radical intermediates are called radical substitution reactions. One of the examples of free radical substitution reaction is the chlorination of methane in the presence of ultraviolet light, shown below.

CH₄ (methane) + Cl₂ —U.V. light→ CH₃Cl (methyl chloride) + HCl

In above reaction, hydrogen atom of the methane molecule is replaced by a chlorine atom (a free radical).

16.3.2 Mechanism of Free Radical Substitution Reactions

We will discuss the mechanism of chlorination of methane to methyl chloride. The mechanism involve the following steps:

Step-1: Initiation: A chlorine molecule undergoes homolytic fission in the presence of ultraviolet light to give chlorine free radicals.

Cl₂ —U.V. light→ 2Cl•

Step-2: Propagation: (a) A chlorine free radical attacks the methane molecule to give methyl free radical and HCl.

Cl• + H–CH₃ → HCl + •CH₃

(b) The methyl free radical, thus produced attacks a chlorine molecule to form methyl chloride and chlorine free radical.

Cl₂ + •CH₃ → Cl• + CH₃Cl

These propagation steps are repeated again and again.

Step-3: Termination: The above chain reaction comes to an end, when any two free radicals combine to form stable products.

Cl• + Cl• → Cl–Cl

•CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃–Cl

•CH₃ + •CH₃ → CH₃–CH₃

In actual practice the above reaction does not stop at methyl chloride stage. The remaining three hydrogen atoms of methyl chloride can be successively replaced by chlorine atoms.

CH₃–Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + HCl

Cl₂ + •CH₃ → Cl• + CH₃Cl

16.2.4 Relative Stability and Reactivity

(a) Alkanes

Alkanes are quite inert and unreactive towards most of the reagents under ordinary conditions. That is why they are also called paraffins. The word paraffin is derived from Latin words parum affinis (little affinity or little reactivity) and testifies to the low reactivity of alkanes. The little reactivity of alkanes is attributed to saturated nature and presence of non-polar C–C and C–H sigma bonds. Consequently polar reagents do not react with alkanes under normal conditions. Furthermore, the C–H and C–C bonds are strong bonds and hence alkanes are relatively stable to common reagents such as acids, alkalies, reducing and oxidizing agents etc. at ordinary conditions. However, they can react with several reagents, if the right conditions are used. The characteristic reactions of alkanes are free-radical substitution reactions.

(b) Cycloalkanes

Cycloalkanes resemble alkanes in their chemical behaviour except for cyclopropane and cyclobutane. The strength of bond and hence the stability, depends on the extent of overlap of orbitals. In the case of cyclopropane and cyclobutane, the extent of overlap of orbitals is not maximum due to greater angle strains and are unstable (Section 16.2.3.2). Cyclopropane undergoes ring opening reactions with several reagents to give open chain addition product. Cyclobutane, having less angle strain than that of cyclopropane, is more stable and hence it undergoes ring opening reaction only under severe conditions. For example, hydrogenation of cyclopropane and cyclobutane to corresponding open chain alkanes in the presence of nickel catalyst, occurs at 80°C and 200°C respectively. Higher members are even more stable and do not undergo ring opening reactions. Instead, they resemble open chain alkanes in reactivity and undergo only radical substitution reactions.

16.3 Radical Substitution Reactions

16.3.1 Overview

Substitution reactions are those reactions in which an atom or group of atoms, attached to the carbon in a molecule is replaced by another atom or group of atoms. A substitution reaction may be initiated by free radical, nucleophile or electrophile. Substitution reactions which involve free radical intermediates are called radical substitution reactions. One of the examples of free radical substitution reaction is the chlorination of methane in the presence of ultraviolet light, shown below.

CH₄ (methane) + Cl₂ —U.V. light→ CH₃Cl (methyl chloride) + HCl

In above reaction, hydrogen atom of the methane molecule is replaced by a chlorine atom (a free radical).

16.3.2 Mechanism of Free Radical Substitution Reactions

We will discuss the mechanism of chlorination of methane to methyl chloride. The mechanism involve the following steps:

Step-1: Initiation: A chlorine molecule undergoes homolytic fission in the presence of ultraviolet light to give chlorine free radicals.

Cl₂ —U.V. light→ 2Cl•

Step-2: Propagation: (a) A chlorine free radical attacks the methane molecule to give methyl free radical and HCl.

Cl• + H–CH₃ → HCl + •CH₃

(b) The methyl free radical, thus produced attacks a chlorine molecule to form methyl chloride and chlorine free radical.

Cl₂ + •CH₃ → Cl• + CH₃Cl

These propagation steps are repeated again and again.

Step-3: Termination: The above chain reaction comes to an end, when any two free radicals combine to form stable products.

Cl• + Cl• → Cl–Cl

•CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃–Cl

•CH₃ + •CH₃ → CH₃–CH₃

In actual practice the above reaction does not stop at methyl chloride stage. The remaining three hydrogen atoms of methyl chloride can be successively replaced by chlorine atoms.

CH₃–Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + HCl
